remarks: Walk through a piece of woodland where birds are not disturbed and your presence will immediately be noticed by the area’s bird community. Most species melt away silently, having been programmed from birth to be wary of the upright Homo sapiens silhouette. But a few will vocalise to communicate the arrival of a trespasser to a mate – standard practice for a Hooded/Carrion Crow or a Magpie – but only Great and Blue Tits will approach for a closer look. Having registered your presence, they then classify the level of threat which they decide you constitute. If, when first spotted, you are not within what they regard as their bailiwick and are proceeding without stopping, they are usually content with ‘passive’ calls that are no more than beacons of sound meant for a partner. But when you enter an invisible exclusion zone they upgrade chit-chat to a ‘something’s up’ communication. This, in both Blue Tit and Great Tit, takes the form of churring. Because the sound reminds me of an engine revving (especially for Blue Tit) I prefer to describe it as revving, rather than churring. Blue Tit revving rises in pitch and then falls and slows down with its terminal note being distinct. Great Tit revving is flat throughout, without any rise or fall or discernible terminal note. Examples of revving from both species are on this clip:XC202487. So far, the birds’ lexicon of sounds express little more than agitation. However, further development to an alert may follow. Now, various types of sounds become options and an individual bird can mix and match between them. It is not clear if there is an actual hierarchy with one type of alarm carrying more weight than another. But it is possible to break down the sounds into categories. One is a fast ‘double-tap’ that sounds like ‘ich-ich’ (or similar). This seems to serve as a panic button and is especially used when a Great Tit or Blue Tit is taken unawares. The call is rapid and the structure of the sound (a fast double-note) rather than the actual sound, is also used as a panic button by several other species, such as House Sparrow, Chaffinch and Blackbird. However, in both tits, the utterance can be given singly or run together into a burst of up to eight or more syllables. Whatever the number of syllables, there is an unmistakable feel of alarm in the broadcast. If a bird is not taken unawares but, instead, is actively monitoring a trespasser, it may employ a different warning. In the case of Blue Tit this is a vibrating trill that is attached to two or three introductory notes. The trill sounds musical and benign and (to my ears) is almost the same as a Blue Tit’s song. Great Tits seem to instil a heightened state of alert by including sudden high-pitched ‘spikes’ after bursts of revving. These are fast and shrill and have a ricochet quality. Great Tits, while in a state of high dudgeon, sometimes also utter other high-pitched musical notes. Maybe these are a kind of vocal monogram, designed to let a partner know that the source of alarms is coming from its mate. Finally, Great Tits have a final joker-card in their arsenal but it is beyond human hearing as well as that of a Sparrowhawk, the presence of which triggers the call. The sound is ultra-sonic and somewhere between a screech and a hiss [XC287261]. Because it carries an imperative to flee immediately, Great Tits also use this call as a false alarm, such as to scare other small songbirds away from a feeding station, leaving the Great Tit to help itself to food.   On the clip, some of the above sounds can be heard. BLUE TIT social calls (that lack alarm intent) are at 0:01, 0:07, 00:12 and a ‘song-alarm’ is at 0:34. GREAT TIT revving is at 0:04, 0:06 and 0:09. A double-tap alarm is at 0:16; single-tap alarms are at 0:20, 0:25 (faint) and 0:31.  Higher-pitched (more frenetic) taps become a trill at 0:23. Great Tit revving can be heard at 0:27 and at 0:37. Just after 0:35, revving changes pitch, or a second Great Tit revs. A pair was present, so it is quite likely that one bird is followed by the other (if so, the first caller is the male in this pair). Finally, this male threw in a series of toy-like double-notes in the middle of his alarms (0:37 and 0:39). These notes were structured like song-notes, that is, a high note followed immediately by a lower note.    RING-NECKED PARAKEETS call at 0:24 and 0:29.

remarks: The Great Tit was watching me because I paused below tall deciduous trees overhanging the steps leading between the upper and lower levels of Helgoland. To begin with I was not interested in the Great Tit (at least two others were nearby) because I was watching a Pied Flycatcher among the same tree canopy. The Great Tit started to scold me by uttering typical churring notes (I prefer to describe the sound as 'revving'). Because it was so close I decided to try and make a recording. I left my recorder below the Great Tit and continued watching the Pied Flycatcher. About 40 seconds later I noticed a Sparrowhawk drift past, just above tree height. I was lucky to be looking in the right direction at the right time, otherwise I would not have recorded the unbelievably fast reaction to the hawk by the Great Tit, which uttered a very high-pitched call that, when you hear it, also has multiple elements at lower pitch too. Great Tits are believed to be able to broadcast calls in a higher register than a Sparrowhawk can hear. The function of such calls is to communicate the danger to other Great Tits nearby. Because, apparently, the sound is so high-pitched, it is only audible to other Great Tits. More discussion about Great Tit's vocabulary is contained within this Facebook post: https://www.facebook.com/anthonymcgeehan/posts/774623669332083:0

remarks: Tanto el observatorio de la Rocina como el del Alcebrón tienen un ecosistema parecido, salvo que en este último hay un palacio del primer tercio del siglo XX que la gente también va a visitar. Ambos lugares están bastante preparados, tienen observatorios para aves en las lagunas, puentes en los arroyos y caminos de tablas para un cómodo desplazamiento de los observadores. El ecosistema es bosque de pino y encina, en la Rocina predominan los primeros mientras que en el Alcebrón las segundas, alternados con lagunas y arroyos que se secan en verano y que están jalonados de vegetación palustre y de ribera tal como todo tipo de carrizos y juncos, árboles típicos de ribera, cañas y helechos. Lo cierto es que algo que llama la atención es que tanto en un bosque como en otro el arbolado está más enfermo de lo que debería, pues los pinos tienen mucho ramaje seco y se ven bastantes encinas muertas.
